content.figure_caption: Diagnostic algorithm for patients with suspected pulmonary embolism without haemodynamic instability. CTPA = computed tomography pulmonary angiography/angiogram; PE = pulmonary embolism.
content.algorithm_summary: 1) Assess clinical probability of PE (clinical judgement or prediction rule). 2) If low or intermediate probability (or PE unlikely): perform D-dimer test. If D-dimer negative → no treatment. If D-dimer positive → CTPA; if CTPA shows no PE → no treatment; if CTPA confirms PE → anticoagulation treatment. 3) If high clinical probability (PE likely): proceed to CTPA directly; if CTPA confirms PE → treatment; if CTPA negative in a high-probability patient → no treatment or further investigation with additional imaging before withholding PE-specific treatment.
key_recommendations_and_notes: When using a moderately sensitive D-dimer assay, restrict measurement to patients with low clinical probability or a PE-unlikely classification; highly sensitive assays may be used in patients with intermediate clinical probability due to higher sensitivity and negative predictive value.
Plasma D-dimer measurement is of limited use for suspected PE occurring in hospitalized patients.
CTPA is considered diagnostic of PE if it shows PE at the segmental or more proximal level.
In case of a negative CTPA in patients with high clinical probability, consider further imaging before withholding PE-specific treatment.
Proposed diagnostic strategy for pregnant women with suspected acute PE is discussed separately (section 9).
content.section_7.1.1_suspected_PE_with_haemodyn: In haemodynamically unstable patients the clinical probability is usually high. Differential diagnoses include cardiac tamponade, acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, acute valvular dysfunction, and hypovolaemia. The most useful initial test is bedside transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) to look for evidence of acute right ventricular (RV) dysfunction; echocardiographic evidence of RV dysfunction in a highly unstable patient may be sufficient to prompt immediate reperfusion without further testing.
